claims.text: The MgAlCuZnGd alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Induction melting produces the alloy in a non-equilibrium state.
The initial alloy is predominantly a supersaturated single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy contains minor secondary phases.
High-temperature exposure drives diffusion-mediated decomposition of the metastable alloy.
Aging or oxidation near 800°C transforms the initial microstructure into a dual-phase microstructure.
The evolved microstructure contains finely distributed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Preferential oxidation of the Mg-rich precipitates forms a coherent, continuous Mg-based oxide scale.
The Mg-based oxide scale acts as a barrier to further high-temperature oxidation.
The Mg-based oxide scale acts as a barrier to corrosive attack in a chloride environment.
The aged alloy will exhibit less oxidation mass gain than the as-cast alloy.
The aged alloy will exhibit a lower salt-spray corrosion rate than the as-cast alloy.
The evolved dual-phase microstructure directly improves both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance.
The proposed mechanism extends to similar Mg-containing lightweight alloy systems with densities below 6 g/cm3.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described both as predominantly single phase with minor secondary phases and as a single-phase baseline that transitions to a bi-phasic state. The presence of initial secondary phases makes the asserted single-phase-to-dual-phase transition imprecise.

The hypothesis wording attributes decomposition to both high-temperature oxidation and corrosive exposure, whereas the specified corrosion exposure is at room temperature and the mechanism attributes decomposition specifically to diffusion during high-temperature exposure.
